stories.title: Israel to give verdict on Netanyahu in pivotal election
stories.summary: A deeply divided Israel heads to the polls for the first time since Hamas's 7 October 2023 attack, with voters delivering their verdict on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the country's rightward drift. Israelis are casting their ballots in the shadow of three years of multi-front regional wars triggered by 7 October, with the trauma still fresh and questions over accountability and security central to the campaign. The close-fought vote comes as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by a devastating military campaign in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank, along with a move towards hard-right religious nationalism. The last opinion polls to be published showed Mr Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, running neck and neck with his main centrist rival Gadi Eisenkot, a political novice and former military chief whose mild manner is seen as the antithesis of the incumbent. Mr Netanyahu is campaigning on his wartime leadership and his alliance with US President Donald Trump, who has endorsed him and joined Israel in waging war on Iran. Mr Netanyahu said yesterday that Mr Trump was prepared to act again to "finally" remove the Iranian threat, but only if Mr Netanyahu remained in power. Mr Eisenkot has accused Mr Netanyahu of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies and threats," and said he was confident Trump would work "in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people."

stories.title: Yellow alerts issued for tomorrow as 5,000 without power
stories.summary: Status Yellow weather warnings will come into effect for 11 counties tomorrow, as around 5,000 homes and businesses remain without power following Storm Boelo. The second named storm of the season brought some very disruptive weather across the country over the last 24 hours, with impacts including power outages, spot flooding, fallen trees and road closures. Air and ferry travel were also affected, with disruption to services continuing into today. Dublin airport operator daa said gusting winds in Ireland and poor weather at airports abroad saw 30 flights cancelled at Dublin Airport today. "While wind speeds have now dropped considerably in the Dublin area, poor weather conditions at other airports mean further disruption is possible," an update from the airport said. The head of the National Directorate for Fire and Emergency Management (NDFEM) Keith Leonard thanked all the local teams from across the country "who worked throughout the last few days to help us to prepare to meet the challenges of Storms Austen and Boelo, mitigate their effects and remedy any impacts afterwards".

stories.title: Minister says meeting with solicitors likely next week
stories.summary: The Minister for Justice has confirmed that he has "engaged" with solicitors and that a meeting is likely next week. Speaking at the launch of One In Four's annual report, Jim O’Callaghan said letters had been exchanged. A majority of solicitors working in criminal legal aid across the country have been in dispute with Mr O'Callaghan since a new €520 flat-fee payment for legal aid cases was introduced in July. Mr O’Callaghan insists that legal aid continues to be granted by the courts; solicitors continue to provide representation, and defendants continue to receive legal services throughout the State. This week, the minister said he would meet the Law Society of Ireland regarding the dispute. In a letter to President of the Law Society of Ireland Rosemarie Loftus, Mr O'Callaghan said he had instructed his officials to "organise a meeting in the coming days to hear your viewpoint and specific concerns".

stories.title: Why you may find the Tuesday after a bank holiday such a downer
stories.summary: Analysis: How you feel after a bank holiday weekend, or any weekend for that matter, can be a reflection of how you view work and your free time A long bank holiday weekend offers a lot of potential. It's the perfect time to go on a break, have an extra day to relax or spend more time with family and friends. While bank holidays usually leave people feeling more refreshed, others may be returning feeling down, or wondering how the days went by so quickly. If you fall into the latter camp and find such feelings happening regularly, there can be several factors in play. One obvious area to look at is work. If you’re feeling down upon your return or you believe the benefits of a long-weekend disappeared the moment you clocked in, then it’s worth analysing why. "If coming back to work is a problem, it could mean two things: the subjective feelings are enlarged, or work is becoming harder for people," said Dr Bert van den Bergh, former associate professor at The Hague University of Applied Sciences and co-author and co-editor of The Social Pathologies of Contemporary Civilization. "What’s really happening is circumstantial." Not everyone shares the same job or career - for example, a 9-to-5 office worker will feel differently than someone who works shifts in retail - so the day you return to work may not matter. What may make a difference is how well you're able to keep your work and personal life separate in your mind. Some may find great meaning from their work, but that can end up overriding other aspects of your life. "One of the things I’ve noticed is that some people just generally have a good boundary with work and not working," said Dr Kelly Dickson, associate professor in Global Health and Wellbeing at University College London and an Integrative Psychotherapist in clinical practice. "Whether it’s four days or three days, they can retain that boundary quite well and that line between when you’re working and not working is stronger for some people than it is for others."

stories.title: Brand 'treated women poorly', says former assistant
stories.summary: Russell Brand's former personal assistant told a court she saw women being mistreated by the comedian and quit working for him when she was "sick of him". Helen Berger worked closely with Mr Brand from June 2006 to February 2007, when he worked on MTV, Channel 4 and BBC as wrote a book and performed stand-up to sell-out crowds. She told Southwark Crown Court that Mr Brand found random women online to satisfy his "insane sexual appetite", but sex often made him depressed. In a statement to Mr Brand’s rape and sexual assault trial, Ms Burger said she saw him "treat women poorly" and accused those close to him of "normalising bad behaviour". She said in a statement read to the court: "Though I’ve worked with a lot of celebrities before and seen a lot of people normalising bad behaviour, this was on another level." She said: "Normalising and dismissing Russell’s behaviour made me think, 'this is just the way it is here'".

stories.title: Carbery's return to fitness and form timed to perfection
stories.summary: When Joey Carbery's time at Bordeaux had been ended by a torn ACL in February, it looked as though his return to Leinster would be significantly delayed. Recovery from anterior cruciate ligament injuries can take anywhere from nine to twelve months and returning too early carries an increased risk of re-rupture. It seemed as though Leinster would have to think more deeply about who would be Sam Prendergast’s back-up when the young out-half is away with Ireland. Harry Byrne and Caspar Gabriel were also available to Leo Cullen. Even with the departure of Ciaran Frawley, Carbery’s return to his home province raised questions about the role he would play when he arrived back in Dublin. His long-term injury added to that uncertainty. However, the final month of Carbery’s rehabilitation brought a dramatic change in circumstances. As expected, Prendergast was named in Andy Farrell’s Ireland squad. Byrne had also been ruled out due to a concussion sustained in the earlier rounds of the United Rugby Championship in South Africa. With no return date announced, questions remain over when Byrne will be available again. Carbery hasn’t always been fortunate with the timing of his injuries. His time in Munster had been affected by multiple issues. His involvement at the 2019 World Cup with Ireland was also hindered by a lingering ankle injury. This time around, his return to action with Leinster might come at the most fortuitous time. Prendergast missed last weekend’s clash with Munster. Whether he was due to play or not was unknown, though there is speculation that he may be facing a few more weeks in the medical room.

stories.title: London SHC: Last-gasp heroics see Brothers Pearse win
stories.summary: Last-gasp heroics from Malcolm Flannery saw Brothers Pearse dig deep and come from behind in injury time to win their 13th London Senior Hurling Championship title and break Sean Treacy’s hearts at McGovern Park in Ruislip. The opening 10 minutes of the decider were fiercely contested. Sean Treacy’s, chasing their first title since 2002, landed the first blow through Adam Jordan before Brothers Pearse’s Paul Kennedy replied in the eighth minute. That would be the north-west Londoners’ last score for more than 10 minutes as their opponents from south of the river began to find their rhythm in a stop-start game. Jack Fagan restored Treacy’s lead with a monster effort, followed by two points from Danny Buckley. Jordan and Michael Roche then stretched the south Londoners’ advantage to five. Kennedy registered his side’s second point in the 20th minute to interrupt Treacy’s scoring run. Another Roche point followed before Eoin O’Neill’s side sparked into life. Kennedy, Aidan O’Brien and Flannery added points before some lovely interplay between Kennedy and O’Brien created an opening for Mark Kilgannon, who superbly flicked the ball into the net to leave just a point between the sides as the interval approached.

stories.title: Shels secure Europa Cup spot despite late Galway rally
stories.summary: All-Island and FAI Cup winners Shelbourne secured second place and a spot in the UEFA Women's Europa Cup for next season as they shared the spoils with Galway United in a bruising battle to bring the curtain down on another Women’s Premier Division season. First half goals from Alex Kavanagh and Isabella Flocchini had Shels in cruise control but two injury-time goals from Emma Doherty and Lucy Jane Grant saw Galway rescue a point in dramatic fashion but proved too little too late as Shels better goal difference saw them over the line. It all came down to this, a straight shootout for the much coveted second place. If a week-long wait of nerves and anticipation wasn’t bad enough, an extra day delay due to the stormy conditions only whetted appetites further. With what turned out to be a crucial the ace up their sleeve of a better goal difference, a draw would have been enough for the visitors prior to kick off but with their hostile hosts itching at revenge for the All-Island Cup defeat at Tolka Park, the double winners knew they couldn’t rest on their laurels. At a blustery Eamonn Deacy Park, it was Phil Trill’s who looked to draw first blood causing an almighty goalmouth scramble that saw both Isabella Beletic and Abbie Callanan have shots blocked as the Reds - wearing white - bodies were thrown on the line. The visitors began to get a foothold and enjoyed large spells of possession but were met by the physical box-midfield of the home side as Amanda McQuillan remained untested early on.

stories.title: Former Ireland prop Phil O'Callaghan dies aged 83
stories.summary: Former Ireland international prop Phil O'Callaghan has passed away at the age of 83, his local club Dolphin RFC confirmed on Sunday. The Cork man won 21 caps for his country between 1967 and 1976, while also representing his province of Munster on 34 occasions, featuring in the first Munster team to beat Australia in January 1967. It was in that same year that he won his first cap for Ireland, also against Australia, in Lansdowne Road. "Everyone at Irish Rugby is saddened to learn of the passing of Phil O'Callaghan. We extend our sympathies to Phil's family, friends and former team-mates at this sad time," the IRFU said in a statement. Born and raised in Cork, O'Callaghan was not an early arriver to rugby. He played hurling, football and soccer in his teenage years, before joining Dolphin at the age of 16, debuting in the second row. From there he played with Dolphin, Munster and then Ireland, while also lining out for the Barbarians six times across 1969 and 1970.

stories.title: Wexford Festival Opera - watch The Gambler by Sergei Prokofiev
stories.summary: We proudly present a live presentation from this year's Wexford Festival Opera - The Gambler by Sergei Prokofiev, with a libretto by the composer after Fyodor Dostoevsky. With its jagged, modernist score, The Gambler offers a chillingly relevant look at the price of desire. Place your bets on a night of operatic intensity and join us for this rare, visceral revival. Written in 1917 during the First World War when the composer was 26 years old and still considered to be in his enfant terrible phase, the opera was not performed until 1929. Based on Fyodor Dostoevsky’s 1866 novella, in this new production – marking the Wexford debuts of director Ivan Popovski and conductor Valentin Uryupin – nervous obsession spirals into self-destruction. Set in 1865 in the fictional German spa town of Roulettenburg, everything is deliberately artificial. The opera follows the protagonist, Alexei, a young tutor, as he spirals into gambling debt while being obsessed with his employer’s stepdaughter, Polina. In the final act, the casino itself emerges as the central character, controlling the destiny of those consumed by their passion for the roulette wheel, like moths to a flame. Prokofiev intended the work as a reaction against Romantic lyricism, instead preferring to create ‘an opera in the declamatory style’, closer in technique to the stageworks of Dargomyzhsky and Mussorgsky which set musical prose in natural speech rhythms. Find out more about this year's Wexford Festival Opera programme here

stories.title: Mel Brooks stars in new short film by Irish director
stories.summary: An LA-based Irish director and producer has pulled off a coup by casting Mel Brooks in a starring role in his new animated short film. Nigel Tiernan, who is originally from Kilkenny but has lived in California since 2009, co-produced Addicted To It, a cautionary tale about mobile phone use in which Brooks, who celebrated his 100 birthday last June, plays a mischievous phone that comes to life and who will do anything to keep its owner hooked. The seven-minute short is currently touring film festivals around the world and has qualified to be considered for the upcoming Oscars in the Animated Shorts category, prior to the announcement of the final shortlist. Addicted To It sees main character, Dace, try to take a walk among the Redwoods without his phone only to have the device turn into 'Phoney Bunny', who tries to pull him back down the rabbit hole of doom scrolling. Brooks, whose long career as a director and writer includes The Producers, Blazing Saddles and Space Balls, was all in on the project as soon as he was sent the concept. Speaking from his home studio in LA, Tiernan (42), who previously worked on Shrek Forever After, The Croods, and Kung Fu Panda 3, says, "When we stumbled onto the bunny character as the idea, it was this notion of something that is charming and sweet but also chaotic.

stories.title: Brown family to pursue public inquiry at UK Supreme Court
stories.summary: The family of murdered GAA chairman Sean Brown will attend the UK's highest court today in pursuit of a public inquiry into his 1997 murder. They will travel to the UK Supreme Court in London for a hearing where Northern Secretary Chris Bryant is challenging a court order requiring him to establish such an inquiry. The case is a long-running and controversial one which has seen the Brown family attend court on up to 60 occasions. Previous court disclosure has revealed that a number of British state agents were among 25 people linked by intelligence to the loyalist murder plot. Mr Brown's daughter Siobhán said the family "never wanted to be here in the first place" and the British government should have adhered to the direction of the court. She said her mother had asked a previous Northern Secretary, Hilary Benn, not to make the family travel to London in pursuit of justice after Northern Ireland's courts found in their favour.

stories.title: Man's body was in Clondalkin facility for days - gardaí
stories.summary: Gardaí have appealed to the public to assist in identifying a man whose body they believe was at a recycling centre in Dublin for a number of days. The man's body was found at the Greyhound Recycling Centre in Clondalkin before 1am yesterday. The scene of the recycling centre has been examined and a post-mortem has been completed. Gardaí said the results are not being released for operational reasons. The investigation team are seeking the public's assistance in trying to identify the man. He is described as being aged between 20 to 50 years years old, of a slim build, white complexion, brown/blonde hair and has no tattoos.

stories.title: No measure can ease pain of scoliosis failures - minister
stories.summary: The Minister for Health has acknowledged that no measures the Government may introduce will alleviate the pain endured by those affected by failures in spina bifida and scoliosis services. She told the Dáil that stakeholders will be consulted by her officials, who will work with the Attorney General to draft terms of reference for a commission of inquiry. The minister was speaking during Statements on Children's Health Ireland (CHI), which was also attended in the visitors' gallery by some of those who have been advocating for action on the matter. Ms Carroll MacNeill said that she received the final scoping report on 9 September, and expressed her gratitude to Remy Farrell SC for his efforts to "capture the pain" and "very real frustration" of those affected. She noted that a commission of investigation, as recommended by Mr Farrell, allows for greater flexibility than a tribunal, including private hearings. She noted that witnesses can request whether to have their testimony heard in public or private.

stories.title: Last remaining slate quarry prepares to resume exports
stories.summary: Ireland's last remaining slate quarry is preparing to resume exports, with an order for 30 tonnes of roofing slate due to be shipped to California in the US. Valentia Slate, which first opened on Valentia Island in 1816, is one of the oldest businesses in the country. More than 200 years later, the business continues to operate underground in the Co Kerry countryside. Slate from the quarry has been used to roof and floor some of the world's most famous buildings, including the Houses of Parliament in London, Westminster Abbey and Cathedral, and Paris Opera House. A rockfall in 1911 forced the closure of the quarry until 1991, but the last five years have seen significant investment in automation. Geologist Aidan Forde is the current owner of Valentia Slate.

"We trust that the Venezuelan authorities and all political actors will seize this opportunity to advance an inclusive, Venezuelan-led dialogue towards free and fair elections," he added. Ms Machado said she is ready to meet the country's interim president. She landed in Caracas yesterday, drawing jubilant crowds in a direct challenge to the US-backed government.

stories.summary: Tuesday's meeting at Galway has been cancelled after further heavy overnight rain at the Ballybrit race course. The third day of Galway's Bank Holiday meeting was originally meant to take place on Monday but due to Storm Boelo all three days of the meeting were put back by 24 hours. However, further rain fell overnight at the track and race organisers have been left with no option but to cancel the day's racing. A short statement from the IHRB read: "Following 12mm of rain overnight and rain continuing at present, the track at Galway is unfit for racing and the fixture scheduled for today has been cancelled."

stories.title: Cork SFC: Fourth time lucky for Nemo Rangers
stories.summary: Nemo Rangers are the McCarthy Insurance Group Premier Senior Football champions for the first time since 2022 after edging passed rivals St Finbarr’s in front of 7,054 spectators at SuperValu Páirc Uí Chaoimh. This comes on the back of three consecutive final defeats, with this victory going down as the club’s 24th overall success. Managed by Robbie O’Dwyer – son of Kerry legend Mick – Nemo got the job done with a performance that saw eight different scorers and Mark Cronin top the charts with eight points. Nemo never trailed against the defending champions, despite a late rally involving goals from Brian Hayes and John Wigginton Barrett reducing the gap down to the bare minimum. The kingpins of Cork football did more than survive in the final moments. They were cool in possession and clinical up front as they found four points to get them over the line in injury time. This was endemic of a statement performance that saw the club storm in front at 0-7 to no score. Mark Cronin contributed four points, including an orange flag into the Blackrock End in the 14th minute.

Both players had golden chances to give their side the lead with Deossa hitting the crossbar just after half-time and then Parrott pulling the ball wide with just Ionut Radu to beat in injury time. "Unfortunately Troy (Parrott) struck it with the instep, very much across goal and the ball just went wide. The team's second half was very good," Pellegrini told DAZN after the match. He added: "We played with Deossa there because it was a back three defense. "Troy played four matches with his national team in three weeks. We have to manage him carefully.

stories.title: McMillan: 'Powers that be' to look at foul play incident
stories.summary: Munster head coach Clayton McMillan said "the powers that be" will decide on the outcome of an allegation of serious foul play, after his side's 24-18 defeat to Leinster at Aviva Stadium. Munster's injury-hit squad felt the full force of Leinster's internationals in the second half of their interpro, as McMillan's side saw their 13-0 lead wiped out by four Leinster tries. There was a major flashpoint late in the first half, when Munster's Gavin Coombes alleged he had been grabbed in the groin by an unnamed Leinster player at a ruck. Referee Andrew Brace stopped play during the 39th minute and spent some time speaking to his TMO, who searched for footage of the alleged incident to no avail. While the officials weren't able to identify the incident during the game, it may still be referred to the citing commissioner. "It's one of those things that we leave in the hands of the powers that be," Munster head coach McMillan said.

stories.title: They did not go quietly - inside Ireland's last witch trial
stories.summary: It’s May 2026 and we are driving on a sunny weekday afternoon to the Islandmagee Peninsula, twenty miles north of Belfast. As the waters of Larne Lough, the body of water which separates Islandmagee from the mainland, comes into view the question arises, what do we believe really happened here on this remote spit of land back in 1711? The history books tell us that a young Presbyterian woman named Mary Dunbar was showing all the signs of demonic possession. Over a period of days, she named eight local women as witches, claiming they were responsible for her torment. The people of Islandmagee, at that time mostly Presbyterians of Scottish descent, believed Mary's accusations and the eight women were arrested, put on trial and found guilty. They are on record as fiercely protesting their innocence in court. Today the peninsula is a tourist attraction for visitors to the Gobbins, a cliff walkway suspended over the Irish Sea. Yet, there are traces of its past written into the landscape; stone built cottages clinging to hillsides, churches dating back to the 1500s, and a landmark steeped in folklore: the Witches’ Rocking Stone, a boulder overlooking Brown’s Bay.

stories.title: Winehouse was 'maybe the greatest lyricist of generation'
stories.summary: Mark Ronson has remembered the late Amy Winehouse as "so funny, so charming, so charismatic' and suggested she was "maybe the greatest lyricist of her generation" ahead of the 20th anniversary of her Back to Black album. The Grammy-winning producer, 51, worked with Winehouse on several tracks from her acclaimed 2006 record, including Rehab, You Know I'm No Good, and the title track. Winehouse, who died in July 2011 aged 27, also featured on Ronson's 2007 cover of Valerie. Ronson recently led a tribute concert alongside producer Salaam Remi and the Amy Winehouse Band at London's Roundhouse, to commemorate 20 years since the album was released on 27 October 2006. Reflecting on his "inspiring' friend and collaborator during Jo Whiley's BBC Radio 2 show on Monday, Ronson said: "It's a wonderful thing to be part of, to see everyone on stage celebrating her, her life, and her music. "Amy just was so inspiring – especially to UK artists. This whole thing is very emotional."

stories.title: Embracing the history, flavours, and spectacular views of Türkiye
stories.summary: Tara Povey experiences the crystal-clear waters, ancient ruins and delicious flavours of Türkiye. Turkey officially became Türkiye in 2022, and I didn't even notice. Despite Istanbul sitting on my travel bucket list for years, I’d never visited. I knew the trope of people going to Türkiye with receding hairlines or dodgy teeth and coming back looking like reality TV stars, but that’s as far as my knowledge went. Then, one day, after some dramatic romantic ups and downs that you may have read about, I met a kind, handsome Turkish man and suddenly I was learning about the Ottoman Empire, and how Türkiye sent aid to Ireland during the Famine. At the end of September we visited Türkiye together for the first time. We both knew my melanin-deprived skin would be no match for the Turkish heat during peak summer when temperatures reach up to 40°C. We flew direct from Dublin to Antalya with Sun Express, picked up our rental car and set off to explore the turquoise coast. Konyaalti is a stunning 7km stretch of pebbly beach with crystal-clear water and the Taurus mountains acting as a dramatic backdrop. We stayed in an apartment in Konyaalti just a few minutes' walk from the beach.

stories.summary: Russia and Ukraine have begun a regional ceasefire to allow the start of a humanitarian effort in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, both sides have said, but they continue strikes elsewhere, including the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv. The ceasefire should enable deliveries of aid as well as evacuations from the frontline town in southern Ukraine that is grappling with acute shortages of food and medicine. "As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments," Dmytro Lubinets, the parliamentary commissioner for human rights, said in a Facebook post confirming Russia's timing of its halt. On Telegram, Russia's defence ministry said it stopped shelling in the direction of Ukraine's city of Kherson from 4am Moscow time (1am Irish time), to prepare for the effort in Oleshky, which faces Kherson across the Dnipro River. Mr Lubinets added that the deal was reached in coordination with US First Lady Melania Trump in cooperation with Russia's commissioner for human rights, Yana Lantratova. Elsewhere, new strikes hit the Southern Bridge and subway infrastructure in Kyiv, forcing a suspension of traffic, city officials said.

stories.title: Mothers 'forgotten victims' of Thalidomide - campaigner
stories.summary: A woman who was born with a birth defect as a result of the Thalidomide drug has said her wish on her 65th birthday is for the Government to fast track a State apology. Thalidomide was developed in the 1950s to treat morning sickness during pregnancy but was withdrawn from most markets in 1961 following widespread evidence it was linked to birth defects. However, it continued to be sold in Ireland until 1964. Ms Cassidy, who was born in 1961, described her birthday as "quite special", saying that many survivors will turn 65 this year. "I was baptised in the delivery ward and I'm actually a little bit emotional about this one (birthday) because we've all deteriorated a little bit. I was thinking of my 60th birthday where I walked half of the Dublin Marathon by default, but this year I'd be lucky if I went up to watch it. "I think the reality of this sort of disability creeping up on us maybe faster than we'd ever seen it coming when we led such independent lives. That's definitely not a good place, but I am glass half full". She explained that she is going to a conference this week in the Netherlands on Thalidomide-related disabilities with over 400 people from all over the world.

stories.title: Irish troops should be in new Lebanon mission - McEntee
stories.summary: Irish troops should be deployed to Lebanon as part of a new EU mission and be involved in both peacekeeping and peace enforcement duties, according to the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Defence Helen McEntee. Troops are currently deployed as part of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) but the mission ends at the end of this year following a Security Council vote, and the Defence Forces are due to withdraw by Easter. A new EU mission to replace UNIFIL was passed by EU Foreign Ministers last month, however, Minister McEntee said: "We will not be able to do that if the Triple Lock is not reformed." Asked if Irish troops participating in a peacekeeping role or peace enforcement role, Minister McEntee replied: "It's likely to be both. And it's important to stress that it currently the case now. "There's a misconception, or an attempt to suggest, that our troops are on the ground in one context, and one context only. Our troops are involved in peace enforcement at the moment." Asked if she would use the guillotine to ensure the Triple Lock legislation passes the Oireachtas before Christmas, which would no longer require a UN mandate before Irish troops could be deployed, the minister replied that she did not intend to rush matters but added: "I do plan to and would like to have this done by the end of the year."

stories.title: Anthropic soaring sales, losses put AI frenzy to IPO test
stories.summary: Anthropic has taken a big step closer to a potentially record-breaking IPO, as it revealed steep losses and security concerns that could test investors' enthusiasm for the AI heavyweight. AI has captured investors' imagination with the promise of a technological leap that could transform businesses, accelerate scientific breakthroughs and unlock vast productivity gains. That has fueled enormous investments in computing infrastructure and AI development, while also stoking skepticism over the scale and pace of the spending. Anthropic's listing comes at a critical time for global markets as investors closely assess whether the billions of dollars being poured into the technology will generate returns to justify sky-high valuations. "There is still enormous excitement about AI's potential to transform businesses, turbocharge productivity and reshape entire industries, but investors are becoming more discerning," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club. Anthropic's net loss in the first half of 2026 widened sharply to $80.7 billion, largely due to a non-operating item related to bonds convertible into the company's shares.

stories.title: N Korea sends letter to UN slamming Seoul over blast
stories.summary: North Korea sent a letter to the United Nations Security Council accusing Seoul of fabricating a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers, its state media reported. Tensions between the two Koreas have soared since the South last month blamed the blast inside the heavily fortified Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) that separates the countries on landmines laid by the North, an accusation it has fiercely rejected. The North Korean permanent representative to the United Nations sent a letter to the UN Security Council regarding the "provocation the ROK committed by groundlessly shifting the blame for the dubious 'mine explosion incident'". The letter said that the landmine incident "fabricated by the ROK, is a sinister obstructive move to brand as a 'military invasion', delay and impede the DPRK's fortification of its southern border," using the acronyms for both countries' official names. The incident was a "farce to evade the responsibility for the ever-escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula," it added. It went on to say its ongoing border fortification efforts were "a legitimate and just exercise of its sovereignty going in strict conformity with the UN Charter," while blasting South Korea for firing warning shots at soldiers involved in the work.

stories.title: NFL: Prescott lifts Cowboys to victory against the Eagles
stories.summary: Dak Prescott threw three touchdown passes, Javonte Williams ran for a career-high 155 yards and the Dallas Cowboys pulled away for a 38-21 away win against the Philadelphia Eagles. The Cowboys (3-4) ended a two game losing run as Prescott passed for 212 yards with two touch downs to CeeDee Lamb and one to George Pickens. They racked up a season-high 204 rushing yards and outgained their NFC East rivals 416-321. The Eagles (2-5) have dropped five straight for the first time since 2016. One week after learning that Jalen Hurts was out for the season with blood clots, Philadelphia put up an early fight and briefly led in the third quarter before allowing 18 unanswered points. Making his fourth NFL start, Tanner McKee threw for 211 yards with a touchdown to Makai Lemon and one interception. Saquon Barkley was used cautiously after missing two games with a hamstring injury, turning nine touches into 71 yards from scrimmage and a rushing score. McKee started the second half with a 17-play, 84-yard drive that took 9:16 off the clock, capping it with a 4-yard touch down toss to the rookie Lemon for a 21-20 Eagles lead. It was all Dallas after that. Prescott floated a 16-yard touchdown pass to Lamb and then ran in the two-point conversion to put the Cowboys up 28-21 late in the third quarter - the game's sixth lead change.
